title: St Theodore the Studite and the See of Rome
subtitle: The appeals of a confessor in exile to the first of the thrones, made inside the order of five, not above it.
summary: St Theodore the Studite wrote to the Bishop of Rome in the highest language a Byzantine could use, and those letters are quoted today as a proof of papal supremacy. Read whole, they are the appeals of a persecuted confessor to the one apostolic throne still free to act, sent alongside letters to Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and aimed at a synod. With the canons of Nicaea and Trullo, Basil's letters in the Arian crisis, Gregory the Great on the universal title, and the definition of the Seventh Ecumenical Council.

essay.text: A young Orthodox Christian meets the quotation somewhere online, usually stripped of its letter, its date, and its author's circumstances: a saint of our own Church writing to the Bishop of Rome, calling him the good shepherd, acknowledging the keys, begging him to save the Church of the East. The first feeling is often a kind of vertigo. Have we been kept from something? The answer is no, and the way to see it is not to explain the saint away but to read him whole. St Theodore the Studite is ours. His letters are ours. Nothing in them needs to be trimmed, and nothing in them needs to frighten us.
The abbot who wrote from exile

In 815 the Emperor Leo V revived the war on the holy icons. The Patriarch Nikephoros was driven from his throne and shut away, and the man raised up in his place, Theodotos Kassiteras, was a layman of the emperor's party. The monasteries took the weight of the persecution: floggings, prisons, exile, and for some of Theodore's brothers, death. Theodore, abbot of the Stoudios monastery, wrote from one place of confinement after another, and his letters travelled by monks who risked their lives to carry them. Of the five patriarchal thrones, Constantinople had been handed over to the heresy, and Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem lay under Muslim rule and could not have answered a summons if they wished to. Rome alone stood outside the emperor's reach, and Rome had kept the faith of the icons. So Theodore wrote to Rome. He also wrote to Alexandria and to Antioch, sending the two of them one and the same letter, and to Jerusalem, because a lawful council needed all of them. That detail is the whole question in miniature: the famous letters to Rome are one part of a canvass of the whole Church.
What he asked Rome to do

He asked for a council. He had written to Rome before, to Pope Leo III, during the earlier crisis in which an imperial marriage the canons forbade was blessed by a priest and then quietly accommodated by the hierarchy. In the icon persecution he wrote to Pope Paschal I, with four other abbots joining their names to his, and asked him to stretch out his hand, and to let it be heard under heaven that by him the presumptuous ones had been synodically accursed. That adverb carries the sentence. Even at the very height of the appeal, the instrument Theodore has in view is a synod, and the outcome he wants is a judgement that the whole Church can receive. The honour he pays along the way is enormous, and it is sincere. He calls the Pope master and apostolic father, he acknowledges him as holder of the keys and as corner-stone of the Church, and he addresses him in the words of the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. A man in chains, writing to the one bishop on earth who could still act freely, does not measure out his reverence in the careful clauses of a legal text. He gives everything he has, and then he asks for a synod.
The order of the five thrones

By Theodore's century the Church in the East reckoned her visible order in five patriarchal thrones: Rome first, then Constantinople, then Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. That order is canonical, not sentimental. Nicaea had regulated the great sees by their ancient customs and by region, and the canons of Trullo say plainly that the see of Constantinople has equal privileges with the see of Old Rome and is second after it. Theodore writes from inside that order, and he does put Rome first; he says so, and we should not clip his words to make him easier for us. But first among thrones is not sole holder of the Church's authority, and Theodore's letters also describe the Church's body as having five heads, which is the Byzantine picture of the pentarchy and not the picture of a single ruling see. Scholars working from the whole correspondence rather than from short extracts point out that he could write to the throne of Jerusalem, honouring it for the ground on which the Lord suffered, in language as high as anything he sent to Rome. High address is the register of a Byzantine letter written under duress. It is real reverence, and it is not a juridical definition. St Basil had written the same way in the Arian persecution, in a letter the manuscripts leave without an address and which is traditionally assigned to Damasus of Rome, asking that men of one mind with him be sent to reconcile the divided churches. The same Basil, on another day, refused to move his judgement because a letter had come from the West, saying that even if it had come down from heaven itself he could not reckon its sender in communion with the saints unless that man agreed with the sound doctrine of the faith. Both letters are Basil's, and neither cancels the other. Rome herself had said something similar in her own voice, when Gregory the Great refused the title of universal bishop and recorded that none of his predecessors had ever consented to use it.

When the icons were vindicated it was not by a decree issuing from one throne. The Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 787 defined their veneration with the legates of Pope Hadrian present and the Eastern patriarchates represented as far as the times allowed, and the Church received that definition as her own. The second iconoclasm outlived Theodore. He died in 826, and it was in 843, under the Empress Theodora and the Patriarch Methodios, that a synod at Constantinople restored the holy images and gave us the Sunday of Orthodoxy. None of this is said to diminish Rome. Rome stood firm through both iconoclasms, and Theodore's gratitude for that is among the warmest things in his letters. But gratitude to a throne that kept the faith is not the same as the claim that a throne cannot fail, and the Church had already anathematised a Pope of Rome by name at the Sixth Ecumenical Council. Read whole, Theodore leaves us no proof text and something better than one, a rule of life: confess the image of Christ, keep the canons, honour the apostolic thrones, ask for help without shame when you are alone, and let the Church judge together what belongs to the faith of all. He wrote all of it from prison. We can at least read him carefully.

florilegium.author: St Theodore the Studite
florilegium.work: Letter to Pope Paschal I, in the rendering of Alice Gardner, Theodore of Studium: His Life and Times (London: Edward Arnold, 1905)
florilegium.reference: At Gardner's account of the appeal to Paschal, Internet Archive scan page 219 of the 1905 edition
florilegium.text: 'And thou when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren'; now is the time and place; help us according to the command received from God. Stretch forth thy hand as far as thou canst; thou hast power from God in that thou art above them all. . . . Good shepherd, lay down thy life for the sheep. . . . Let it be heard under heaven that by thee the presumptuous ones have been synodically accursed.
florilegium.gloss: The appeal at its highest pitch, and the thing asked for is a synodical condemnation. Theodore, with four other abbots, writes to the one apostolic throne outside the emperor's reach. The ellipses are Gardner's own.

florilegium.author: The Council in Trullo (the Quinisext)
florilegium.work: Canons of the Council in Trullo (692)
florilegium.text: Renewing the enactments by the 150 Fathers assembled at the God-protected and imperial city, and those of the 630 who met at Chalcedon; we decree that the see of Constantinople shall have equal privileges with the see of Old Rome, and shall be highly regarded in ecclesiastical matters as that is, and shall be second after it. After Constantinople shall be ranked the See of Alexandria, then that of Antioch, and afterwards the See of Jerusalem.
florilegium.gloss: The canonical shape of the world Theodore inhabited: an ordered college of thrones, named in order, with equal privileges spoken of in the same breath as precedence.

florilegium.author: The First Ecumenical Council, Nicaea
florilegium.text: Let the ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail, that the Bishop of Alexandria have jurisdiction in all these, since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also. Likewise in Antioch and the other provinces, let the Churches retain their privileges. And this is to be universally understood, that if any one be made bishop without the consent of the Metropolitan, the great Synod has declared that such a man ought not to be a bishop. If, however, two or three bishops shall from natural love of contradiction, oppose the common suffrage of the rest, it being reasonable and in accordance with the ecclesiastical law, then let the choice of the majority prevail.
florilegium.gloss: The great sees are regulated by ancient custom and by region. Rome is named alongside Alexandria and Antioch as the pattern, not above them as their governor, and the canon ends by letting the majority decide.

florilegium.author: The Seventh Ecumenical Council, Nicaea
florilegium.work: The Decree of the Second Council of Nicaea (787)
florilegium.reference: NPNF Second Series, vol. 14. This is the opening of the definition; the sentence continues on the page.
florilegium.text: We, therefore, following the royal pathway and the divinely inspired authority of our Holy Fathers and the traditions of the Catholic Church (for, as we all know, the Holy Spirit indwells her), define with all certitude and accuracy that just as the figure of the precious and life-giving Cross, so also the venerable and holy images, as well in painting and mosaic as of other fit materials, should be set forth in the holy churches of God, and on the sacred vessels and on the vestments and on hangings and in pictures both in houses and by the wayside
florilegium.gloss: The cause Theodore suffered for was defined by a council of the whole Church, with Roman legates present and the Eastern thrones represented. This is the instrument he was asking Rome to help him obtain again.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.work: Letter 70, headed in NPNF "Without address" and traditionally assigned to Damasus of Rome
florilegium.text: But, as I was disappointed, I have been constrained to beseech you by letter to be moved to help us, and to send some of those, who are like minded with us, either to conciliate the dissentient and bring back the Churches of God into friendly union, or at all events to make you see more plainly who are responsible for the unsettled state in which we are, that it may be obvious to you for the future with whom it befits you to be in communion.
florilegium.gloss: Four and a half centuries before Theodore, an Eastern Father under persecution writes westward for help in exactly the same shape: send men, help us, make the truth of our situation plain.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: I shall never be able to persuade myself on these grounds to ignore Meletius, or to forget the Church which is under him, or to treat as small, and of little importance to the true religion, the questions which originated the division. I shall never consent to give in, merely because somebody is very much elated at receiving a letter from men. Even if it had come down from heaven itself, but he does not agree with the sound doctrine of the faith, I cannot look upon him as in communion with the saints.
florilegium.gloss: The same Basil who asked the West for help will not surrender his judgement to a letter from it. Appeal and submission are not the same act, and the Fathers did not confuse them.

florilegium.author: Pope St Gregory the Great
florilegium.work: Registrum Epistolarum, Book V, Epistle 43, to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch
florilegium.text: For, as your venerable Holiness knows, this name of Universality was offered by the holy synod of Chalcedon to the pontiff of the Apostolic See which by the providence of God I serve. But no one of my predecessors has ever consented to use this so profane a title; since, forsooth, if one Patriarch is called Universal, the name of Patriarch in the case of the rest is derogated. But far be this, far be it from the mind of a Christian, that any one should wish to seize for himself that whereby he might seem in the least degree to lessen the honour of his brethren.
florilegium.gloss: Rome's own witness to how such titles were understood: exalted address is honour among brethren, and a Pope of Rome refuses to let it be read as universal office.

florilegium.author: St Cyprian of Carthage
florilegium.work: Treatise 1, On the Unity of the Church
florilegium.text: And although to all the apostles, after His resurrection, He gives an equal power, and says, As the Father has sent me, even so send I you: Receive the Holy Ghost: Whose soever sins you remit, they shall be remitted unto him; and whose soever sins you retain, they shall be retained; yet, that He might set forth unity, He arranged by His authority the origin of that unity, as beginning from one. Assuredly the rest of the apostles were also the same as was Peter, endowed with a like partnership both of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity.
florilegium.gloss: The principle under all of it: Peter is the origin and type of unity, and the apostolic college shares his honour and his power.

scripture.note: Strengthen thy brethren, the verse Theodore sets at the head of his plea to Pope Paschal, applied as a summons to act, not as a grant of jurisdiction.
Upon this rock, the text at issue in every reading of these letters.
Feed my sheep, the charge Theodore presses on Rome and which the Fathers press on every shepherd.
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, the words Theodore turns into an appeal from prison.
The apostolic pattern of decision, the council, which is what Theodore was asking for all along.

editorialNotes: WHAT I VERIFIED THIS RUN. Every florilegium entry that remains was fetched from its own source URL during this review and compared word for word against the proposed transcription. Verified exact and unchanged: Council in Trullo canon 36, Nicaea I canon 6, the opening of the Nicaea II definition, and St Basil Letter 70. Verified and then corrected: St Basil Letter 214, Pope St Gregory Book V Epistle 43, St Cyprian On the Unity section 4, and the St Theodore passage from Gardner. Nothing was added from memory. No entry was deleted, because every one of them proved to be genuinely present at a reachable source once the errors below were fixed.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, most serious. The Gregory the Great entry cited the wrong letter and the wrong URL. The draft pointed at newadvent.org/fathers/360207043.htm, which is Book VII, Epistle 43, addressed to Marinianus of Ravenna, and does not contain the universal-title passage at all. The correct text is Book V, Epistle 43, to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch, at newadvent.org/fathers/360205043.htm. The draft's wording was also altered: it dropped the opening clause 'For, as your venerable Holiness knows,', dropped the word 'forsooth', collapsed 'But far be this, far be it from the mind of a Christian' into a single 'far be this', and lowercased 'Patriarch' twice. The entry now carries the URL and the exact wording as printed. A reviewer should confirm the NPNF volume number, given here as Second Series vol. 12.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED. The Basil Letter 214 entry misquoted the decisive clause. The draft read 'but the bishop does not agree with the sound doctrine of the faith'. The text reads 'but he does not agree with the sound doctrine of the faith'. Two words were inserted that are not Basil's, in the one sentence the whole entry exists to carry. Corrected. The rest of the passage verified exact.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED. The Cyprian entry had been silently modernised: 'his resurrection', 'he gives', 'he might set forth', 'he arranged' where the ANF text has 'His' and 'He', a semicolon before 'yet' where the text has a comma, and a comma inside the quotation from John where the text has a semicolon. The text now matches the page. Separately, a rights and scholarship point the drafter missed: chapter 4 of On the Unity survives in two ancient recensions, and the other one contains the primacy language about the chair of Peter. A study specifically about Roman claims should not cite this chapter without a clergy reviewer knowing the chapter is textually contested. Consider a one-line framing note, or drop the entry.

DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED. The Gardner citation was wrong. The draft cited p. 183. The passage is not there. It is at Internet Archive scan page 219 of the 1905 edition, inside Gardner's narrative of the appeal to Paschal. Cross-checking her index entries against the scan gives a consistent offset of 32 between scan leaf and printed page in this part of the book, which would put the printed page near 187, not 183. I have not asserted a printed page number in the citation. A reviewer with the physical book or the page images should fix the printed page and then the reference can be tightened.

GARDNER, TEXT VERIFIED. The quoted words were confirmed verbatim against the Internet Archive full text of the 1905 edition, including the two sets of ellipses, which are Gardner's own. One change was made: her text reads 'as far as thou canst; ' followed by a dash, and the dash was dropped under the no-em-dash house rule. No words were altered, added, or reordered. If a reviewer prefers strict typographic fidelity to the house rule, restore the dash or drop the entry.

GARDNER, SURROUNDING CLAIMS NOW VERIFIED. Three load-bearing claims that the draft flagged as unverified were confirmed against the same page. Gardner states that Theodore joined the names of four other abbots to his own; that he addressed the Pope as Master and Apostolic Father and acknowledged him as possessor of the keys and corner-stone of the church; and that, with the idea of a synod in mind, he wrote also to the Patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch, sending them an identical letter, and to the Patriarch of Jerusalem. The essay's central structural claim therefore rests on a verified public-domain source and no longer needs an independent check for its existence. It still deserves a check against the Greek.

GARDNER, STILL OPEN. She gives no letter number for the passage, and she is a non-Orthodox Cambridge historian writing in 1905. Someone with PG 99 or the Fatouros edition should identify the letter and check her rendering against the Greek before this ships. Her rendering is the only reason we can quote Theodore at all in this study.

HISTORICAL ERROR FOUND AND FIXED IN THE ESSAY. The draft said that after Nikephoros was deposed in 815 'a compliant bishop was installed in his place'. Theodotos Kassiteras was a layman, not a bishop, which is precisely why his elevation was scandalous. Gardner states this plainly. The essay now names him and says layman. This matters to the argument, since it is part of why the domestic hierarchy could not be appealed to.

UNVERIFIED CLAIM WEAKENED IN THE ESSAY. The draft asserted that Theodore had asked Pope Leo III 'either to call a synod of lawful authority or at the least to send a letter that would carry weight'. I could confirm from Gardner only that Theodore corresponded with Leo III and that the later letter to Paschal was shorter than the one formerly sent to Leo. The specific content of the request to Leo III could not be verified in a public-domain source this run, so the essay now says only that he had written to Leo III during the earlier marriage crisis. If a reviewer can source the specific ask, it can be restored.

COPYRIGHT. The clause about Jerusalem was rewritten in this pass. The draft read that Theodore addressed Jerusalem 'for the sake of the place where the Lord suffered', which tracks the wording of Meyendorff's translation too closely for a copyrighted work that is supposed to be framing only. It now reads 'honouring it for the ground on which the Lord suffered'. A reviewer should still read that clause with Meyendorff open and confirm it is a description and not a rendering.

COPYRIGHT, carried over from the drafter and still binding. The quotations that circulate most widely in this debate, the rock of faith on which the Catholic Church is built, You are Peter adorning the throne of Peter, the five-headed body of the Church, the passage about the Supreme See in which Christ placed the keys of faith, and the address to the Patriarch of Jerusalem as first among the patriarchs with the dignity highest of all, reach English only through copyrighted modern translations. They are absent from both essay and florilegium and must stay absent. If clergy want any of them, they need a fresh translation from PG 99 or explicit permission. Do not let one be pasted in from an apologetics site.
EM DASHES. Checked every field of the output. There are none. The only one in play was inside the Gardner quotation and it was removed as described above.

POLEMIC. Two phrases were softened in this pass. The draft's 'Historians who have read the whole correspondence rather than the anthologised extracts' carried a sneer at the people being answered and has been made neutral. The draft's characterisation of the earlier crisis as 'an imperial adultery' has been restated as a marriage the canons forbade, which is accurate and less inflammatory in a study a Catholic reader may open. Nothing from the source Discord thread's combative register survives: not the checkmate framing, not the claims about apologists' motives, and not the Pratsch material describing the saint as an arrogant and stubborn fanatic.

DOCTRINAL WORDING NEEDING A SECOND PAIR OF EYES. (a) 'first among thrones is not sole holder of the Church's authority': confirm this states the Orthodox position on Roman primacy accurately and generously. (b) The study concedes, following Gardner, that Theodore in practice gave Rome a weight above the other thrones and says so in his own words. That concession is deliberate and honest; a priest should confirm we want it stated so plainly. (c) The section 'The order of the five thrones' describes the pentarchy as the Church's visible order in that century. It must not read as though the pentarchy were a dogma. Please check the phrasing. (d) The claim that Theodore's letters describe the Church's body as having five heads is stated in our own words but is known to us only through copyrighted translations. Confirm we are comfortable asserting it without a quotable source.

BASIL LETTER 70 ATTRIBUTION. The draft called this 'Letter 70, to Damasus of Rome'. NPNF heads it 'Without address'. The identification with Damasus is traditional and probably right, but it is an inference and the study now says so, both in the entry and in the essay. Left as it stands, the earlier version would have overstated what the source says.

HISTORICAL DETAILS STILL TO CONFIRM against a reference the app trusts: the deposition of Patriarch Nikephoros in 815; the dating of the letter to Pope Paschal I, usually placed around 817, which this draft deliberately does not state; Theodore's repose in 826; the restoration of the icons in 843 under the Empress Theodora and the Patriarch Methodios; and the description of the Eastern patriarchates as represented at Nicaea II, where the credentials of the two Eastern monks were irregular and the essay's hedge 'as far as the times allowed' is doing real work.

The essay refers in one clause to the anathema of a Pope of Rome by name at the Sixth Ecumenical Council, meaning Honorius in 681. It is accurate and it is already in papacy.json, but if clergy would rather this study stay off that ground it can be cut without weakening anything.

NICAEA II QUOTATION IS A TRUNCATION. The words quoted are exact, but the sentence continues on the page with the enumeration beginning 'to wit, the figure of our Lord God and Saviour Jesus Christ'. The entry stops mid-sentence without an ellipsis, which is noted in its reference field. If house style wants a trailing ellipsis or the full sentence, that is an editorial call, not an accuracy one.

NICAEA I CANON 6 was extended in this pass to include its closing sentence about the choice of the majority prevailing, which was verified along with the rest and which supports the conciliar point the study is making. Trullo canon 36 was likewise extended to include its closing sentence naming Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem in order, since the study's argument is about the whole order and not only about Rome and Constantinople.

LINKING. No saint profile exists at data/saints/theodore-the-studite, so no saintSlug is set for the study's own subject. Adding one would make this study link properly and should probably happen before ship. The only saintSlug used is basil-the-great, which exists. Both related slugs, papacy and filioque, exist in data/theology. Note that papacy.json references saintSlugs that are not present in data/saints; that pattern was not copied here.

STORAGE SHAPE. This output has no councils array, so the three conciliar texts sit in the florilegium with the council named as author. If this is stored as data/theology/theodore-the-studite-and-rome.json, move Trullo canon 36, Nicaea I canon 6 and the Nicaea II definition into a councils array with councilSlug values, to match the existing files.
estimatedMinutes was lowered from 16 to 13. It is still an estimate, not a measurement.

REMAINING SPOT-CHECK. Basil Letter 214, Gregory Book V Epistle 43 and Cyprian section 4 were carried into the draft from data/theology/papacy.json. Three of those three needed correction here, which means the copies sitting in papacy.json are very likely wrong in the same ways. Someone should re-verify those entries in papacy.json against their sources before the next release, and check whether papacy.json is also pointing at the Marinianus letter for Gregory.

CYPRIAN SECTION 4, RE-VERIFIED THIS RUN, THE FLAG WAS A FALSE POSITIVE. scripts/verify-florilegium.mjs scored this entry 52 of 102 words. I fetched newadvent.org/fathers/050701.htm with curl, stripped the tags, and compared the quotation word for word against the page. All 102 words are present, in order, with no substitutions and no reordering. The run breaks at word 52 for one reason only: New Advent splices the inline scripture reference 'John 20:21' into the middle of the ANF text, between 'they shall be retained' and 'yet, that He might set forth unity'. That is site apparatus, not Cyprian and not the ANF translator, and it stays out of the quotation. The entry is kept as genuine. Its work, reference, source URL and gloss are unchanged.

CYPRIAN SECTION 4, ONE PUNCTUATION MARK RESTORED. The page prints a semicolon at the point where the spliced reference sits: 'they shall be retained; John 20:21 yet, that He might set forth unity'. The draft carried a comma there. With the apparatus removed, the faithful reading is a semicolon, so the comma before 'yet' has been changed back to a semicolon. This is not an em dash case and the house rule does not apply to it. No word was added, removed, reordered, or respelled. This is the only change made to the entry.

CORRECTION TO AN EARLIER NOTE IN THIS FILE. The earlier Cyprian note claims the draft had 'a semicolon before yet where the text has a comma'. That is backwards, and it is what introduced the comma now reverted. The page has the semicolon. The rest of that note is sound: the His and He capitalisations do match the page, and so does the internal punctuation of the quotation from John. Its substantive warning also stands untouched by this run, that chapter 4 of On the Unity survives in two ancient recensions and the other one carries the chair of Peter primacy language, so a clergy reviewer should still decide whether a study about Roman claims cites this chapter with a framing note or drops it. Verifying the words does not settle that question.

SCHEMA NOTE, ACTION NEEDED ON REASSEMBLY. The return schema for this pass has no modernScholarship field, so the four framing-only entries in the staged file (Meyendorff, Siecienski, Dvornik, Pratsch, each marked not quoted) could not be carried through this output. That is a limitation of the return shape, not a deletion I made. Re-attach that array unchanged from the staged file before this ships, or the drafting trail behind the copyright notes above is lost.

SCOPE OF THIS RUN. Only the Cyprian entry was flagged and only the Cyprian entry was touched. The other seven florilegium entries, the essay, the scripture list, the related slugs, and every pre-existing editorial note were carried through byte for byte and were not re-fetched. There are no Ostroumoff entries in this study; that instruction belongs to council-of-florence.json.

modernScholarship.work: John Meyendorff, Byzantine Theology: Historical Trends and Doctrinal Themes
modernScholarship.usedFor: Framing only. Supports the reading that Theodore's exalted address to Rome belongs to a Byzantine register of honour, that he speaks elsewhere of the Church's body as five-headed, and that he addressed the See of Jerusalem in comparably exalted terms. Named so an editor can trace the drafting. Not quoted anywhere in this study, and the sentence about Jerusalem was rewritten in this pass specifically to stop tracking Meyendorff's phrasing.

modernScholarship.work: A. Edward Siecienski, The Papacy and the Orthodox: Sources and History of a Debate
modernScholarship.usedFor: Framing only. Supports the reading that Theodore's praise of Rome arises from his need to enlist Roman support under persecution and his gratitude when it came, while he continued to hold the pentarchic ideal. Not quoted.

modernScholarship.work: Francis Dvornik, Byzantium and the Roman Primacy
modernScholarship.usedFor: Framing only. Supports the points that Theodore recognised the emperor's customary right to convoke councils, that he urged referral to Rome when no council was called, and that he attributed apostolic character to all the patriarchal sees. Not quoted.

modernScholarship.work: Thomas Pratsch, Theodoros Studites (759-826): zwischen Dogma und Pragma
modernScholarship.usedFor: Background on Theodore's career and on how the Constantinopolitan establishment regarded him. Its judgements about his personal ambition and character were deliberately not carried into this draft. Not quoted.
